chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Harun ibn Muslim, from Mas'ada ibn Sadaqa, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) sent to a man five wasqs of Al-Bughayba dates, and the man was among those who hoped for his voluntary gifts and anticipated his support, and he did not ask Ali (peace be upon him) or anyone else for anything. A man said,
A man to Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him): 'By Allah, So-and-so has not asked you, and one wasq from the five wasqs would have sufficed him.'

So Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) said to him: 'May Allah increase the number of believers! You are stingy while I am giving. For the sake of Allah, if I do not give to the one who hopes for me except after he asks, and then I give him after he asks, I have not given him the cost of what I have taken from him. And that is because I have exposed him to risking his face, which he places on the ground for my Lord and his Lord, during his worship of me and his seeking of his needs from me.'

So whoever does this to his Muslim brother, knowing that he is a recipient of his charity and kindness, and does not confirm Allah in his supplication for him, where he wishes for him Paradise with his tongue but is stingy with him over the chaff of his wealth, then that is because the servant may say in his supplication: 'O Allah, forgive the believing men and the believing women.' If he supplicates for them with forgiveness, he has asked for Paradise for them. So how just is he who does this with his tongue and does not confirm it with his action?

key_terms.أَوْسَاقٍ: wasqs (plural of wasq, a unit of volume/weight for dates)
key_terms.الْحُطَامِ: the chaff (metaphor for small amounts of wealth)
key_terms.يُعَفِّرُهُ فِي التُّرَابِ: to place it on the ground (prostration/humility)

ai.seo_question: Why did Imam Ali give more than asked to someone who didn't ask?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam Ali (peace be upon him) illustrates the spiritual cost of conditional generosity, noting that withholding charity until asked forces the recipient to humble themselves, effectively 'charging' them for the gift. This act of 'exposing' the brother to need undermines the sincerity of verbal prayers for Paradise, as true faith requires confirming words with material support. The narrative emphasizes that stinginess while claiming benevolence is a form of insincerity that fails to validate one's supplications for the community.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from Haroun Bin Muslim, from Mas’ada Bin sadaqa, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> that Amir Al-Momineen<sup>asws</sup> sent five baskets of Al-Bagheyba dates to a man, and the man was from the ones who hoped for his<sup>saww</sup> voluntary gifts and hoped for attaining these, and his<sup>asws</sup> support, and he did not used to ask Ali<sup>asws</sup> for something nor anyone else. A man said to Amir Al-Momineen<sup>asws</sup>, ‘By Allah<sup>azwj</sup>! So and so has not (even) asked you<sup>asws</sup>, and it would have sufficed him had it been one basket rather than the five (you<sup>asws</sup> have given to him)’.

So Amir Al-Momineen<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘May Allah<sup>azwj</sup> not Make the likes of you to be among the Believers! Why are you exercising the stinginess while I<sup>asws</sup> am the (one<sup>asws</sup> who is) giving it?

For the Sake of Allah<sup>azwj</sup>! You, (listen)!  If I give charity to a person who expects to receive charity from me only after his request, I, in fact, have not given him the cost of what I have already taken from him.  Such cost is my compelling him to risk the dignity of his face, which he places on the ground before my Lord<sup>azwj</sup> and his Lord<sup>azwj</sup> during his worship and his appeal before Him<sup>azwj</sup> for his needs.

With this kind of dealing with a Muslim whom one knows as deserving of one’s charity and gifs, one has not proved oneself as truthful before Allah<sup>azwj</sup>, in one’s prayer when one appeals verbally before Allah to admit one’s Muslim brother into Paradise.  On the other hand, one exercises stinginess in matters of worthless belongings.  This happens when a servant of Allah says in his prayer: O Allah, Grant forgiveness to male and female believers.  Appealing for forgiveness is asking Paradise for male and female believers.  It is unjust not to support one’s words with one’s deeds.
en.sarwar: 1. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from Harun ibn Muslim from Mas’adah ibn Sadaqah who has said the following: “Abu ‘ Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, has said that once, ’Amir al-Mu’minin, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, decided to give five Awsaq (a certain amount of) dates from al-Bughaybighah (a place in al-Madinah) to a man who had hoped to benefit from the generosity of the Imam and his gifts. However, he would not appeal before the Imam or other people for any help. A man said to
’Amir al-Mu’minin, ‘Alayhi al- Salam, ‘This man has not appealed before you. One is enough for him instead of five Awsaq.’

’Amir al-Mu’minin then said, ‘I wish Allah will not create more people like you among the believers. Why do you exercise stinginess about the charity that I have decided to give to a needy person? You must take notice, for the sake of Allah! If I give charity to a person who expects to receive charity from me only after his appeal, I, in fact, have not given him the cost of what I have already taken from him. Such cost is my causing him to risk the dignity of his face, which he places on the ground before my Lord and his Lord during his worship and his appeal before Him for his needs.

With this kind of dealing with a Muslim whom one knows as deserving of one’s charity and gifts, one has not proved oneself as truthful before Allah, the Most Majestic, the Most Glorious, in one’s prayer when one appeals verbally before Allah to admit one’s Muslim brother into Paradise. On the other hand, one exercises stinginess in matters of worthless worldly belongings. This happens when a servant of Allah says in his prayer, ‘O Allah, grant forgiveness to male and female believers.’ Appealing for forgiveness is asking Paradise for male and female believers. It is unjust not to support one’s words with one’s deeds.’”
